speaker: Patrick Hsu
title: Arc Institute's Patrick Hsu on Building an App Store for Biology with AI
question: In computational biology, why are DNA foundation models much harder to prompt effectively than text-based LLMs?
guest: The interesting oxymoron with these models for me is the way that we use them. Just like you use ChatGPT, it's text in, text out. Evo is DNA in, DNA out. And it turns out we don't speak DNA very well. Imagine if you were using a model like ChatGPT in Russian, where only 1% of the words were in English. That's kind of what it feels like—you don't really know what's going on. So you have to build lots of annotators and techniques to try to interpret and read what's happening. The way that we even use and prompt the models is really primitive. Doing fancy prompt engineering workflows to get more utility out of these models is something we're just in the very early innings of exploring with biological language models, because we speak DNA with an extremely heavy accent.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
DNA foundation models are harder to prompt mainly because DNA is not a language humans read or write, so there is no natural way to express intent in it.

Text LLMs are trained on data in which instructions, questions, and answers already appear together, so a prompt can simply describe the task. Genomes contain no such instruction–response structure: nothing in a sequence says "now design a liver-specific enhancer." A prompt can only be a sequence context, such as a species tag, a neighbouring gene, or the start of an element, that makes the desired continuation statistically likely.

Several features of the data compound this. Functional signal is sparse, with most of the genome non-coding, repetitive, or weakly constrained. Meaning is encoded in long-range dependencies spanning thousands to millions of bases. Function also depends on cell type and chromatin state, which the sequence alone does not show.

Finally, you cannot judge the output by reading it. Checking whether a generated sequence works requires predictive models or wet-lab experiments, so prompt iteration is slow and expensive. In practice, people rely on fine-tuning, control tokens, or guided generation instead.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Text LLMs share a compositional, human-readable language in which instructions and outputs use the same medium, reinforced by extensive instruction tuning. DNA foundation models, by contrast, operate over a four-letter nucleotide alphabet with no native syntax for expressing high-level intent; instead of describing a desired trait, users must steer generation implicitly through genomic prefixes, taxonomic tags, or concatenated sequence examples. Because evolved genomes do not naturally contain explicit task instructions or artificially juxtaposed examples, crafted prompts easily fall out of distribution. Genomic semantics are also far less modular than words: biological function emerges from strict reading frames, subtle motifs, 3D chromatin structure, and long-range regulatory interactions across kilobases, while depending heavily on cellular and epigenetic states absent from raw sequence alone. Even single-base shifts can abolish activity, leaving little tolerance for imprecise context. Finally, humans cannot read generated DNA to judge output quality and iteratively refine prompts on the fly, forcing prompt engineering to rely on imperfect predictive oracles or slow, costly wet-lab validation.

noweb.answer: DNA foundation models are much harder to prompt than text-based LLMs primarily because genomic sequences lack a built-in meta-language for expressing instructions. Natural language blends content and intent within the same medium, so text corpora naturally contain questions, explanations, and input-output examples that foster in-context learning. By contrast, a genome is an evolved molecular record of four nucleotides rather than a communicative text; you cannot phrase a task description in raw bases, nor do chromosomes contain few-shot demonstrations for a model to imitate. Furthermore, biological function is non-local and depends heavily on cellular context absent from raw sequence alone. Whether a DNA segment drives gene expression depends on tissue-specific transcription factors, epigenetic states, 3D chromatin folding, and enhancers hundreds of kilobases away. Sequence representation adds further fragility: k-mer or byte-pair tokenization can arbitrarily split short binding motifs, and inserting a single base can shift codon reading frames downstream. Consequently, steering DNA models usually requires explicit conditioning tags, task-specific fine-tuning, or guided decoding rather than intuitive zero-shot prompting.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
DNA foundation models are hard to prompt mainly because DNA has no instruction channel. Text LLMs learned from human language and are often instruction-tuned, so you can simply say what you want. A genomic model like Evo or the Nucleotide Transformer sees only strings of A, C, G and T. The only way to "prompt" it is to supply a starting sequence, such as a gene fragment, a promoter, or a species or taxonomy tag. You have to steer it through statistical context rather than stated intent, much like prompting an early base model with no instruction tuning.

There are other obstacles. What a sequence does depends on things the sequence doesn't contain, like cell type, chromatin state and methylation. Regulatory effects can span tens of thousands of bases or more, beyond what a short prompt can capture. Most of the genome is repetitive or weakly constrained, so the signal is sparse. Humans also can't read DNA well, so you can't easily tell whether a prompt worked. Checking whether a generated sequence actually functions usually needs computational proxies or wet-lab experiments, which makes trying and refining prompts slow and expensive.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
DNA foundation models are much harder to prompt than text-based LLMs primarily because DNA has no built-in meta-language for expressing instructions or task intent. Human text naturally contains questions, definitions, examples, and formatting cues, and text LLMs are further aligned on instruction-following datasets so users can steer them flexibly in plain language. By contrast, genomic sequences consist solely of nucleotide strings shaped by evolution rather than communication, leaving no native way to ask a model to predict a variant's pathogenicity or design a cell-type-specific promoter.

Moreover, biological function is rarely self-contained within a short sequence prompt. Meaning depends heavily on sparse, long-range interactions, 3D chromatin structure, epigenetic state, and cellular environment, making raw nucleotide context an imprecise steering signal. Even when researchers prompt autoregressive DNA models with homologous sequences, species tags, or genomic prefixes, the model simply performs statistical sequence continuation rather than explicit reasoning. Consequently, adapting DNA foundation models to specific tasks typically requires fine-tuning, learned embeddings, or inference-time guidance rather than zero-shot prompting.

noweb.answer:
DNA foundation models are much harder to prompt than text-based LLMs primarily because genomes lack a native instruction language. Human text naturally embeds questions, task descriptions, formatting cues, and input-output examples, enabling LLMs to follow instructions and learn in context. By contrast, DNA consists only of nucleotide sequences shaped by evolutionary and biochemical constraints rather than explicit commands. You cannot tell a DNA model what task to perform; instead, prompting requires supplying a biological motif, homologous sequence, or genomic locus and relying on sequence continuation to yield a functional design.

Moreover, biological function is rarely self-contained in a short linear prompt. Gene regulation and molecular behavior depend on distant regulatory elements, 3D chromatin structure, epigenetic state, and cellular environment—context absent from raw DNA alone. Finally, unlike prose that humans can immediately read and refine, evaluating whether a prompted DNA sequence actually works requires specialized predictive models or wet-lab experiments, making iterative prompt engineering slow and opaque.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Text LLMs can take instructions in the same medium they were trained on: natural language. They also benefit from instruction tuning on examples that show how to turn a request into an answer. Most DNA foundation models are trained on raw sequences, so they learn which patterns tend to occur together. Their training rarely includes examples that connect a user’s intent to a sequence with the desired function.

DNA’s effects also depend on context. The same sequence can behave differently depending on where it sits in the genome, which other regions interact with it, and which cell type it’s in. A short sequence prompt may leave much of that context unspecified. And while a person can often judge whether a text response followed an instruction, confirming that a DNA sequence has the intended effect may require a lab assay. So a sequence can look plausible to the model while doing something quite different in a cell.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Text-based LLMs learn from language that includes questions, instructions, and answers, and many are further trained to follow instructions. DNA foundation models usually learn to predict missing or subsequent bases in genomic sequences. That training can teach a model to recognize biological patterns, but it gives the model little practice interpreting a sequence as a request. There’s no standard DNA equivalent of “predict whether this gene is active.”

Biological context also matters. The same regulatory sequence can have different effects in different cell types because different proteins are present. A DNA prompt alone may therefore omit information needed to answer the question. In practice, researchers often have to define how the sequence represents the task, supply relevant context, and train a task-specific readout to turn the model’s representation into an answer.
